Equal volumes of ideal gas are contained in vessels A and B. A is at 8.1×10⁶ Pa and 18°C; B is at 5.3×10⁶ Pa and 36°C. What is the ratio NA/NB of the numbers of molecules?

evidence.review: Derived independently from the question and checked against the first-assessment2025 IB Physics guide; handwritten annotations are not answer evidence.

answer.text:
Editorial worked explanation, checked against the official mark scheme:

Two separate graph readings give (1.0×10^5 Pa)(12×10^-5 m³) = 12 J and (4.0×10^5 Pa)(3.0×10^-5 m³) = 12 J. Since pV is constant at constant temperature, the air behaves ideally. With pV = nRT, T = 12/[(4.5×10^-3)(8.31)] = 321 K. Temperature tracks mean molecular kinetic energy; pressure comes from molecular momentum transfer at the walls.
answer.evidence: Official mark scheme checked on page 6.

answer.text:
Official answer D checked; editorial worked explanation:

At equilibrium the connected gases have the same pressure. From pV = nRT, mass is proportional to V/T for the same gas. Thus mX/mY = (2V/150)/(V/300) = 4. Therefore D.

parts.display_text: (a) Using Newton’s third law, outline how gas molecules exert pressure on container walls. (b) State one difference between an ideal and a real gas. (c) At the same temperature, 0.20 m³ of ideal gas at 3.0×10⁴ Pa and 0.10 m³ at 9.0×10⁴ Pa are connected. The temperature stays constant. Determine the final pressure.

answer.text: Official markscheme conclusions; editorial worked explanation: (a) A molecule’s momentum changes when it collides with a wall, so the wall exerts a force on the molecule. By Newton’s third law, the molecule exerts an equal and opposite force on the wall. The combined force per unit wall area is the gas pressure. (b) For example, an ideal gas models molecules as point particles with no intermolecular forces, whereas real molecules have finite size and interactions. (c) At fixed T, total amount is proportional to pV. Therefore P(V₁+V₂)=p₁V₁+p₂V₂, so P=[(3.0×10⁴)(0.20)+(9.0×10⁴)(0.10)]/0.30=5.0×10⁴ Pa.

An ideal-gas equation is written pVA = NBT, where N is the number of molecules and A is the Avogadro constant. Kinetic theory also gives pV = Nm⟨c²⟩/3.

(a) State the meaning of T and identify B.
(b) Explain the meanings of m and ⟨c²⟩.
(c) Derive the mean molecular kinetic energy in terms of A, B and T.
(d) Sketch how root-mean-square molecular speed varies with T for this gas.

answer.text:
(a) T is thermodynamic temperature in kelvin; B is the molar gas constant R.
(b) m is the mass of one molecule, and ⟨c²⟩ is the mean of the squared molecular speeds.
(c) Equating pV gives NBT/A = Nm⟨c²⟩/3. Therefore ⟨E_k⟩ = ½m⟨c²⟩ = 3BT/(2A) = 3k_BT/2.
(d) c_rms = √⟨c²⟩ ∝ √T: draw an increasing curve through the origin with decreasing gradient. The extrapolated zero-temperature limit is a mathematical feature of the ideal-gas model.

parts.display_text: A known gas mass M_g is sealed in a clear cylinder under a freely movable piston of mass m_p. Objects each of mass m_o and a metre rule are available. Design measurements to graph density ρ against absolute pressure P at constant temperature. You may use the checked expressions P=P_atm+(m_p+Nm_o)g/(πr²) and ρ=M_g/(πr²h), with cylinder radius r, gas height h and N added objects. Use the experimental graph shown to decide whether the gas behaves ideally.

answer.text: Measure the internal cylinder diameter at several positions and divide by two to find r. Measure gas-column height h from the base to the piston for several counts N of added objects. Add each load slowly and wait for the gas and surroundings to return to the same room temperature before reading; keep ambient temperature steady. Repeat heights for each N and average. Calculate P and ρ using the supplied formulas and plot ρ vertically against P horizontally. At fixed mass and temperature an ideal gas has PV=constant and ρ=M_g/V, so ρ∝P: a straight line through the origin. The observed curved graph is inconsistent with ideal behavior over this range.

answer.text:
Published key D checked; editorial worked explanation:

D. The hemisphere volume is (1/2)(4πr³/3)=2πr³/3, so its weight is (2πr³ρg)/3. The contact area is πr². Hence P=F/A=[(2πr³ρg)/3]/(πr²)=2ρrg/3.

answer.text: Official answer C. Editorial worked explanation: The piston radius is d/2, so its area is A=π(d/2)²=πd²/4. Hence p=F/A=4F/(πd²).
